transcript.content: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, nice to meet you, Doctor. Um, the main reason I’m here is that I'm just really struggling at work lately. I manage a few medical clinics, and anything that takes real, sitting-down brain work... like, we just got this new software system for the patient portals, and honestly, whoever designed the interface clearly has never worked in a health setting. It's all these drop-down menus inside other drop-down menus. My buddy Dave—he works in IT over at the university—he was telling me that vendors do that on purpose to lock you into their support contracts. Which makes total sense, right? Because every time it freezes, we have to call them. Anyway, Dave's actually thinking about buying a pontoon boat this summer, which is crazy in this economy, but... wait, sorry, what was I saying? 

Oh, right, why I'm here. Yeah, so things like doing the monthly clinic reports or trying to plan a big multi-site health event... I just feel like I hit a wall with it. I keep putting it off and putting it off, even when I know it really matters. It's just getting to be a real problem for me.
Have you always had trouble focusing on detailed work like this, or is this something that's gotten worse recently?

Honestly, I think it's always been like this. Even way back in elementary school, my teachers used to tell my parents that I was a bright kid, but I was just always daydreaming. I remember my third-grade teacher, Mrs. Gable—she had this massive collection of ceramic frogs on her desk. I'd just sit there staring at them, wondering who dusts them all. Because you know how dust gets in all the little grooves? My wife collects these vintage teacups, and I keep telling her we need a glass cabinet, but furniture is so expensive right now. Wood prices went up a few years ago and never really came back down, which is just ridiculous. 

But anyway, yeah, my teachers said I was always losing my worksheets and forgetting to turn in my homework. The only way I ever got anything handed in was if my mother checked my backpack every single night. She’d dump it out right on the kitchen table. It was one of those old canvas backpacks with the heavy leather bottom... they really don't make them like that anymore. The zippers on those things were indestructible. My son has gone through three backpacks this year alone, the stitching just falls apart. But um... yeah, to answer your question, it's definitely not a new thing. It's been happening since I was a kid.

Besides the difficulty focusing, have you noticed times when your mood is unusually high or when you feel like you have a lot more energy than normal—maybe where you're talking more, sleeping less, or your thoughts are racing?

No, I wouldn't say I've ever felt like that. I mean, my energy levels are pretty normal, I guess. I definitely don't sleep less... actually, I love my sleep. We just bought this new mattress, one of those hybrid ones with the memory foam and the coils? They ship it to you in this tiny box, and you cut the plastic and it just inflates like a life raft. It's wild to watch. My wife filmed it on her phone because she wanted to put it on Facebook. She's always putting stuff on Facebook, which I don't really get. Like, who cares what we had for dinner on a Tuesday, you know? But she loves it, connects with her cousins back in Ohio. Ohio is beautiful in the fall, by the way. Have you ever been? The leaves change and it's just... gorgeous. But uh, yeah, what were you asking? Oh, right, the energy thing. No, I don't get super energetic or anything like that. Just regular, I guess.
Do you find yourself fidgeting a lot, having trouble sitting still, or feeling restless—like you need to be moving or doing something with your hands?

No, not really. I mean, I can sit still just fine. I'm sitting still right now, right? I don't feel like I'm bouncing off the walls or anything. My brother-in-law, though, he's a knee-bouncer. Every time we go over there for Sunday dinner, the whole table shakes. He's an accountant, so I guess he's just stressed all the time. Tax season really takes it out of him. Last year he got audited himself, which is kind of ironic, isn't it? An accountant getting audited. He said it was a nightmare. They had to pull receipts from like, five years ago. Who keeps receipts for five years? I can barely find the receipt for the dry cleaning I dropped off on Tuesday. I had this really nice blue suit cleaned for a conference, and the tag fell off. The guy at the counter was completely unhelpful. Just looked at me like I was speaking a different language. It's so hard to find good customer service these days. But yeah, no, I don't really have the fidgeting thing. I'm pretty calm physically.
Do you find yourself making quick decisions or doing things without thinking them through first—like interrupting people, saying things you later regret, or acting on impulse?

No, I wouldn't say I'm impulsive. I usually think things through pretty carefully. Like at work—I manage an outpatient clinic—and whenever we have to order new supplies or hire someone, I always take my time. Speaking of hiring, we had this guy come in for an interview last week, and he was wearing this bright yellow tie with little cartoon golf clubs all over it. For an admin position! I mean, who wears a novelty tie to a job interview? I like golf as much as the next guy, but there's a time and a place, you know? 

My buddy Dave and I try to get out to the municipal course on weekends, but it's been raining so much lately that the greens are just completely waterlogged. It's like playing in a swamp. You hit the ball and it just goes *thwack* into the mud and completely disappears. Dave lost three balls last Saturday, and those Pro V1s aren't cheap. He was so mad he almost threw his wedge into the pond. But um... wait, what was the question? Oh, doing things without thinking or interrupting. Yeah, no, I don't really have a problem with that. I'm pretty good at holding back.

When you're working on one of those big projects at the clinic—like planning the multi-site health event you mentioned—do you have trouble getting started, or do you struggle more with organizing your approach and breaking it down into steps?

It's definitely the organizing part. When I’m juggling work projects, the memorial committee stuff I volunteer for, and those outreach events, it gets really messy. The memorial committee is actually trying to get a new bronze plaque made for the park downtown, right by the old fountain. Have you seen that fountain? They finally fixed the plumbing on it last month. For years it just shot water out sideways onto the sidewalk, and people would get completely soaked walking by. My neighbor's golden retriever used to try and drink from it and he'd just get blasted in the face. He's a good dog, though. Buster. Loves tennis balls. But anyway, bronze is so expensive right now, the foundry quoted us double what we paid five years ago. So I've been trying to coordinate the fundraising for that, and... wait, what was the question? 

Oh, right, breaking things down into steps. Yeah, so with all those different things going on, I end up with notes in like three different places. I'll have stuff on my phone, a legal pad on my desk, sticky notes everywhere... and I just look at it all and I can’t seem to figure out what needs to happen first. I can't prioritize it. So I just kind of get stuck, and then I end up rushing at the very end to get everything done before the deadline.

When you're trying to focus on paperwork or sit through a meeting, do you find yourself getting an urge to get up and do something else, or do you feel like you need to move on to the next task even if you haven't finished what you're working on?

No, not really. I mean, I don't get this sudden urge to just jump up and run out of the room or anything. If I'm in a meeting, I stay in the meeting. We have these mandatory staff meetings every Tuesday morning at 8:30, which is just an awful time for a meeting. Half the staff hasn't even had their coffee yet. We get our coffee from this little local roaster down the street, and they do this incredible dark roast. The owner, Marcus, he actually used to work in medical billing before he opened the shop. Talk about a career change, right? Going from staring at insurance codes all day to roasting coffee beans. He said the stress of dealing with Medicare denials was giving him an ulcer. Which I completely understand. The new coding system they rolled out last year is just an absolute nightmare. We had to retrain the entire front office staff. But yeah, no, I don't feel like I need to get up and leave or anything like that. I just sit there until the meeting is over.

I've noticed during our conversation that you tend to go off on tangents and bring up a lot of details that aren't directly related to what we're discussing. Do people in your life—your wife, coworkers, friends—ever mention that you talk a lot or that you jump around between topics when you're telling a story?

I mean, I don't think I'm a big talker in general. But I do notice I start talking way too much when I'm nervous, especially if I feel like I've dropped the ball on something. Like, if I make a scheduling mistake at the clinic, I'll just over-explain exactly how it happened. I'll go on and on, and I can tell the other person already gets it, but I just keep going. 

Scheduling has been a real headache lately anyway. We switched to this new software—supposed to be "cloud-based and intuitive"—but it's a disaster. It keeps double-booking Dr. Henderson. Dr. Henderson is a great guy, really old-school, still uses a dictaphone for his notes. He actually collects vintage medical instruments, he's got this glass case in his office full of these terrifying-looking antique saws and syringes. I asked him once where he finds them, and he said he goes to estate sales on the weekends. My wife loves estate sales, she found this amazing mid-century modern credenza at one last month. It was a steal, but getting it into the back of my SUV was a whole ordeal. We had to take the legs off and everything. 

But um... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, talking too much. Yeah, it's mostly just when I mess up and get anxious, I just kind of word-vomit all the details trying to justify it, even when they've clearly stopped listening.

When you're trying to have a conversation with your wife or someone at work, do you ever find yourself interrupting them or blurting out thoughts before they've finished talking, even though you don't mean to?

No, not really. I don't think I do that. I'm usually pretty good about letting people finish their thoughts. My wife actually says I'm a good sounding board when she needs to vent, especially lately with her sister. Her sister just moved out to Arizona—Scottsdale, I think. Or maybe Tempe? Anyway, she bought this house that has a pool, which sounds amazing, right? But the pool pump broke literally the second week she was there. Have you ever heard a broken pool pump? When the bearings go out, it sounds like a literal jet engine taking off in your backyard. She had to hire this specialized pool technician, and he charged her an absolute fortune because it was some discontinued model from the nineties. 

I told my wife right then, we are never getting a pool. We used to have a hot tub on the back deck, but the wood started rotting from all the moisture. We tried to get it fixed last summer and the contractor we hired just completely ghosted us after tearing half the boards up. Left a giant mess in the yard for months. We finally had to... wait, sorry. What was the question? 

Oh, blurting things out. Right. No, I don't really struggle with that. I usually just wait until there's a pause in the conversation.

When you're actually working on something that requires concentration—like reading through those clinic reports or learning that new software system—can you focus okay once you get started, or do you find your mind wandering even when you're trying hard to pay attention?

Yeah, that's... that's actually a big problem for me. It's like, I can sit down and really want to pay attention, but my brain just won't stay put. Like, if I'm in one of those meetings trying to listen to a budget update—which, let me tell you, those budget meetings are just brutal. Our CFO, Linda, she presents everything in these tiny, unreadable spreadsheets. She uses like, an eight-point font. I told her once she needs to make the text bigger, but she said she likes to see the whole quarter on one screen. Which makes no sense because nobody else can read it. And she always wears these bracelets that clink together when she types, it's so distracting. 

But yeah, I'll be trying to listen to her, and then someone's phone will vibrate on the table, or I'll hear people talking out in the hallway. Or even just... I'll suddenly remember something totally random, like an email I forgot to send for my fantasy football league. I've been running this league for like ten years, and this season is just a mess. Two guys dropped out at the last minute, so we had to scramble to find replacements. My buddy Dave got his brother-in-law to join, but the guy doesn't even watch football. He drafted a retired kicker in the fourth round. We all tried to tell him, but he insisted the guy was a "sleeper pick." 

Anyway, what happens is, I get caught up thinking about the league or whatever distracted me, and by the time I snap back to the meeting, I've completely missed the last three or four minutes of what Linda was saying. And then I have to ask someone for the notes later, which is always embarrassing.

When you were a kid—back in elementary or middle school—did your parents or teachers ever say you were hyperactive, that you were always on the go, or that you seemed to have endless energy compared to other kids your age?

No, I wasn't really a hyper kid. I was pretty quiet, actually. I spent a lot of time reading or just kind of daydreaming. My mom used to say I was always in my own little world. We lived in this house near the woods, and I'd just sit by the window for hours watching the birds. My dad actually built this incredible birdhouse—it looked like a miniature log cabin, he even used real twigs for the roof. He was always building stuff like that. He was a carpenter, mostly did custom cabinetry for kitchens. You know how hard it is to find good custom cabinetry these days? Everything is just that cheap particle board from Ikea. We tried to put an Ikea dresser together for the guest room last year, and I swear, the instructions were basically hieroglyphics. We ended up with three extra screws and the bottom drawer never closed right. 

But yeah... wait, what were you asking? Oh, about being hyper. No, I wasn't running around or climbing the walls or anything like that. I was pretty calm, just... easily distracted, I guess.

You've mentioned struggling with focus at work and having trouble since elementary school. How about at home with your wife—does she notice you having trouble paying attention to her, or forgetting things she's asked you to do? Or is it mainly just a work problem?

Oh, it's definitely not just my main job. My wife notices it all the time at home. She gets pretty frustrated because I'll forget things she's asked me to handle. Like, lately we've been helping organize this community health drive together—she loves volunteering for that stuff. She actually used to run the whole neighborhood committee back at our old house. 

That old house was great, except we had this massive oak tree in the front yard. The roots started buckling the driveway, and the HOA got involved. Have you ever dealt with an HOA? Absolute nightmare. They sent us these certified letters on this thick cardstock paper, threatening to fine us fifty bucks a day. Fifty bucks! For a tree we didn't even plant! We had to hire this arborist, and his truck leaked oil all over the street, which just made the HOA even madder, and then we had to power wash the concrete... 

Wait, sorry, what were we talking about? My wife, right. Yeah, she notices the forgetfulness. Especially with all that volunteer stuff we do. I’ve been forgetting to return calls from volunteers, and I keep missing small errands for the events that she specifically asks me to run. It gets bad. Once or twice I’ve had to apologize because a community meeting completely slipped my mind until someone texted me asking where I was. So yeah, it definitely happens a lot outside of work too.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has significant hyperactivity symptoms (a key feature that would distinguish ADHD Combined Type from Predominantly Inattentive Type), since he has denied obvious motor restlessness but may experience internal restlessness or feel driven to keep moving between tasks
doctor.question: When you're trying to focus on paperwork or sit through a meeting, do you find yourself getting an urge to get up and do something else, or do you feel like you need to move on to the next task even if you haven't finished what you're working on?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the urge to leave one's seat or move on to other tasks before finishing (symptoms of hyperactivity such as leaving seat, or inattention such as failing to finish duties). Neither of these specific symptoms are in my profile.

patient.answer: No, not really. I mean, I don't get this sudden urge to just jump up and run out of the room or anything. If I'm in a meeting, I stay in the meeting. We have these mandatory staff meetings every Tuesday morning at 8:30, which is just an awful time for a meeting. Half the staff hasn't even had their coffee yet. We get our coffee from this little local roaster down the street, and they do this incredible dark roast. The owner, Marcus, he actually used to work in medical billing before he opened the shop. Talk about a career change, right? Going from staring at insurance codes all day to roasting coffee beans. He said the stress of dealing with Medicare denials was giving him an ulcer. Which I completely understand. The new coding system they rolled out last year is just an absolute nightmare. We had to retrain the entire front office staff. But yeah, no, I don't feel like I need to get up and leave or anything like that. I just sit there until the meeting is over.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient has excessive talkativeness/pressured speech characteristic of ADHD, as evidenced by tangential speech patterns and difficulty staying on topic during the interview itself
doctor.question: I've noticed during our conversation that you tend to go off on tangents and bring up a lot of details that aren't directly related to what we're discussing. Do people in your life—your wife, coworkers, friends—ever mention that you talk a lot or that you jump around between topics when you're telling a story?

target_item.name: Excessive_Talking
target_item.manifestation: I notice I start talking too much when I’m nervous about having dropped the ball, like I’ll over-explain a scheduling mistake and keep going even after the other person clearly got the point.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if I talk a lot or if others mention that I talk excessively, which directly corresponds to the Excessive_Talking symptom.

patient.answer:
I mean, I don't think I'm a big talker in general. But I do notice I start talking way too much when I'm nervous, especially if I feel like I've dropped the ball on something. Like, if I make a scheduling mistake at the clinic, I'll just over-explain exactly how it happened. I'll go on and on, and I can tell the other person already gets it, but I just keep going. 

Scheduling has been a real headache lately anyway. We switched to this new software—supposed to be "cloud-based and intuitive"—but it's a disaster. It keeps double-booking Dr. Henderson. Dr. Henderson is a great guy, really old-school, still uses a dictaphone for his notes. He actually collects vintage medical instruments, he's got this glass case in his office full of these terrifying-looking antique saws and syringes. I asked him once where he finds them, and he said he goes to estate sales on the weekends. My wife loves estate sales, she found this amazing mid-century modern credenza at one last month. It was a steal, but getting it into the back of my SUV was a whole ordeal. We had to take the legs off and everything. 

But um... wait, what was I saying? Oh, right, talking too much. Yeah, it's mostly just when I mess up and get anxious, I just kind of word-vomit all the details trying to justify it, even when they've clearly stopped listening.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient meets criteria for ADHD Combined Type (which requires evidence of hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms) or ADHD Predominantly Inattentive Type. The patient shows clear inattention symptoms and tangential speech patterns, but has denied hyperactivity, restlessness, and impulsivity. I need to clarify whether the tangential speech and difficulty organizing/prioritizing reflect executive dysfunction (inattention) or whether there are genuine hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms I may have missed, particularly given the prominent verbal tangentiality observed throughout the interview.
doctor.question: When you're trying to have a conversation with your wife or someone at work, do you ever find yourself interrupting them or blurting out thoughts before they've finished talking, even though you don't mean to?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about impulsivity symptoms, specifically blurting out answers or interrupting others. These symptoms are not present in my profile.

patient.answer:
No, not really. I don't think I do that. I'm usually pretty good about letting people finish their thoughts. My wife actually says I'm a good sounding board when she needs to vent, especially lately with her sister. Her sister just moved out to Arizona—Scottsdale, I think. Or maybe Tempe? Anyway, she bought this house that has a pool, which sounds amazing, right? But the pool pump broke literally the second week she was there. Have you ever heard a broken pool pump? When the bearings go out, it sounds like a literal jet engine taking off in your backyard. She had to hire this specialized pool technician, and he charged her an absolute fortune because it was some discontinued model from the nineties. 

I told my wife right then, we are never getting a pool. We used to have a hot tub on the back deck, but the wood started rotting from all the moisture. We tried to get it fixed last summer and the contractor we hired just completely ghosted us after tearing half the boards up. Left a giant mess in the yard for months. We finally had to... wait, sorry. What was the question? 

Oh, blurting things out. Right. No, I don't really struggle with that. I usually just wait until there's a pause in the conversation.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the patient's primary difficulty is with sustained attention/concentration on tasks versus executive function/organization, to help confirm ADHD-Inattentive type and rule out other possibilities
doctor.question: When you're actually working on something that requires concentration—like reading through those clinic reports or learning that new software system—can you focus okay once you get started, or do you find your mind wandering even when you're trying hard to pay attention?

target_item.name: Distractibility
target_item.manifestation: In meetings, I’ll be trying to listen to a budget update, but a phone vibrating, people talking in the hall, or even a thought about something I forgot for the league pulls me away and I miss the next few minutes.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the mind wandering or losing focus during tasks, which directly corresponds to being easily distracted by extraneous stimuli or unrelated thoughts.

patient.answer:
Yeah, that's... that's actually a big problem for me. It's like, I can sit down and really want to pay attention, but my brain just won't stay put. Like, if I'm in one of those meetings trying to listen to a budget update—which, let me tell you, those budget meetings are just brutal. Our CFO, Linda, she presents everything in these tiny, unreadable spreadsheets. She uses like, an eight-point font. I told her once she needs to make the text bigger, but she said she likes to see the whole quarter on one screen. Which makes no sense because nobody else can read it. And she always wears these bracelets that clink together when she types, it's so distracting. 

But yeah, I'll be trying to listen to her, and then someone's phone will vibrate on the table, or I'll hear people talking out in the hallway. Or even just... I'll suddenly remember something totally random, like an email I forgot to send for my fantasy football league. I've been running this league for like ten years, and this season is just a mess. Two guys dropped out at the last minute, so we had to scramble to find replacements. My buddy Dave got his brother-in-law to join, but the guy doesn't even watch football. He drafted a retired kicker in the fourth round. We all tried to tell him, but he insisted the guy was a "sleeper pick." 

Anyway, what happens is, I get caught up thinking about the league or whatever distracted me, and by the time I snap back to the meeting, I've completely missed the last three or four minutes of what Linda was saying. And then I have to ask someone for the notes later, which is always embarrassing.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient meets criteria for ADHD Combined Presentation by assessing whether inattention symptoms are accompanied by hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms, or if this is purely an inattentive presentation (ADHD-I). The patient has clearly demonstrated inattention and executive dysfunction, but has consistently denied hyperactivity, impulsivity, and restlessness. I need to probe more directly about whether there are any hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms present, particularly in childhood when ADHD is typically most obvious.
doctor.question: When you were a kid—back in elementary or middle school—did your parents or teachers ever say you were hyperactive, that you were always on the go, or that you seemed to have endless energy compared to other kids your age?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about childhood hyperactivity, such as being 'on the go' or having endless energy. My profile does not include hyperactivity symptoms; my childhood symptoms were related to inattention (daydreaming, losing worksheets).

patient.answer:
No, I wasn't really a hyper kid. I was pretty quiet, actually. I spent a lot of time reading or just kind of daydreaming. My mom used to say I was always in my own little world. We lived in this house near the woods, and I'd just sit by the window for hours watching the birds. My dad actually built this incredible birdhouse—it looked like a miniature log cabin, he even used real twigs for the roof. He was always building stuff like that. He was a carpenter, mostly did custom cabinetry for kitchens. You know how hard it is to find good custom cabinetry these days? Everything is just that cheap particle board from Ikea. We tried to put an Ikea dresser together for the guest room last year, and I swear, the instructions were basically hieroglyphics. We ended up with three extra screws and the bottom drawer never closed right. 

But yeah... wait, what were you asking? Oh, about being hyper. No, I wasn't running around or climbing the walls or anything like that. I was pretty calm, just... easily distracted, I guess.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient meets full ADHD criteria by clarifying whether inattention symptoms are present across multiple settings (home, work, social) or primarily in specific contexts, which would help rule out other diagnoses and confirm ADHD-Combined or Predominantly Inattentive Type
doctor.question: You've mentioned struggling with focus at work and having trouble since elementary school. How about at home with your wife—does she notice you having trouble paying attention to her, or forgetting things she's asked you to do? Or is it mainly just a work problem?

target_item.name: Daily_Activities_Forgetfulness
target_item.manifestation: I’ve been forgetting to return calls from volunteers, missing small errands for events, and once or twice I’ve had to apologize because a community meeting completely slipped my mind until someone texted me.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about forgetfulness in daily life, such as forgetting things the patient's wife asked him to do, which aligns with the symptom of daily activities forgetfulness.

patient.answer:
Oh, it's definitely not just my main job. My wife notices it all the time at home. She gets pretty frustrated because I'll forget things she's asked me to handle. Like, lately we've been helping organize this community health drive together—she loves volunteering for that stuff. She actually used to run the whole neighborhood committee back at our old house. 

That old house was great, except we had this massive oak tree in the front yard. The roots started buckling the driveway, and the HOA got involved. Have you ever dealt with an HOA? Absolute nightmare. They sent us these certified letters on this thick cardstock paper, threatening to fine us fifty bucks a day. Fifty bucks! For a tree we didn't even plant! We had to hire this arborist, and his truck leaked oil all over the street, which just made the HOA even madder, and then we had to power wash the concrete... 

Wait, sorry, what were we talking about? My wife, right. Yeah, she notices the forgetfulness. Especially with all that volunteer stuff we do. I’ve been forgetting to return calls from volunteers, and I keep missing small errands for the events that she specifically asks me to run. It gets bad. Once or twice I’ve had to apologize because a community meeting completely slipped my mind until someone texted me asking where I was. So yeah, it definitely happens a lot outside of work too.

opening_question.intent: Establish rapport and elicit the chief complaint to begin differential diagnosis
opening_question.question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient presents with a lifelong history of inattention, poor organization, and difficulty sustaining focus that began in elementary school and persists into adulthood across multiple settings (work, home, volunteer activities). Core ADHD symptoms of inattention are clearly present: mind-wandering despite effort to concentrate, difficulty organizing complex tasks, forgetfulness in daily responsibilities, and easy distractibility by irrelevant stimuli. Notably absent are hyperactivity-impulsivity symptoms—the patient explicitly denies fidgeting, restlessness, impulsivity, and interrupting. The prominent tangential speech and excessive detail observed during the interview, combined with the patient's own acknowledgment of excessive talking when anxious, suggests possible secondary manifestations rather than core hyperactivity. The functional impairment is evident across work (difficulty with detailed reports and project planning) and home (forgotten commitments, missed volunteer meetings). Duration criterion is satisfied by lifelong symptoms since childhood. This clinical picture is most consistent with Predominantly Inattentive Type ADHD in adulthood.
